title: The little way
hook: Thérèse of Lisieux: small things done with great love

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine's five words. Your line was love, then do. When you checked the root of that one act, what did you find? Today, a young nun who took love down to the smallest size. Day eight hundred thirty-five.

In a Carmelite convent in Lisieux, in France, a young nun named Thérèse wanted to be a saint. But when she measured herself against the great saints, she writes, she felt like a grain of sand beside a mountain. She would never do anything that size. She was going to spend her life in a small enclosed house, doing laundry and chores, praying with the same few women every day. So she went looking for another road. Today: the little way.
screen: `A YOUNG NUN WANTS TO BE A SAINT.` → `A GRAIN OF SAND BESIDE A MOUNTAIN.` → `SHE LOOKS FOR ANOTHER ROAD.`

segments.voice: Thérèse tells this in her memoir, Story of a Soul, and the pictures she uses are homely. First, the elevator. She'd heard of elevators, an invention, she notes, that lifted people so they didn't have to climb. She was too small, she writes, to climb the rough staircase of perfection. She wanted an elevator. And she decided it was the arms of Jesus, lifting the little ones who can't climb. Second, flowers. Love, she says, proves itself by deeds, and she had no great deeds to give. So she would strew flowers: every small sacrifice, every glance, every kind word, offered with love. Nothing was too small to count. Third, the hardest one. There was a sister in the convent whose manner, Thérèse admits, she found deeply disagreeable. So she set out to treat that sister as she would the person she loved most. Whenever they met, she smiled, and she prayed for her. One day, she writes, the sister asked her what it was about her that Thérèse found so attractive. Fourth, the center. Underneath all of it is a discovery she writes about: in the heart of the Church, her vocation would be love. Not a role. A way of doing every small thing. Catholics honor her as a saint. Some readers find her way fits small lives: a nurse on night shift, a parent of toddlers, anyone whose day is mostly ordinary. The size of the act, in her way of seeing, isn't the measure. The love inside it is.
screen: `AN ELEVATOR, NOT A STAIRCASE.` · `STREWING FLOWERS.` · `THE SISTER SHE FOUND HARD.` · `HER VOCATION WOULD BE LOVE.` · then, large: `THE LITTLE WAY.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Run through the next few hours in your mind and pick the most ordinary thing waiting in them: a dish, an email, a diaper, a commute, a line at the store. Now picture doing that exact thing with great care, for someone, the way Thérèse strewed flowers. Not faster. Not bigger. Just with love inside it. Notice how small it is, and let that be fine. If you pray, you can offer it, the way she did. The bell holds the time.
The little way. Thérèse of Lisieux's road for small people: ordinary things, done with great love, offered like flowers. Today's word.
Your line: the little way. Today, do that one ordinary thing with love inside it, and tell no one. Day eight hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics who follow Thérèse's little way offer small daily tasks and kindnesses to God, and some ask her prayers as Saint Thérèse, the Little Flower.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gentle saying about being humble.
what it means: a road to holiness for people who can't do great things: small acts, offered with great love, like flowers.
what a scholar hears: Story of a Soul's own pictures, the elevator and the strewn flowers, and her discovery that her vocation, in the heart of the Church, would be love.
